title: Ki Teitzei: the forgotten sheaf (Deuteronomy 24:19)
hookLine: a sheaf left behind by accident belongs to the poor

cards: Harvest day, a long time ago. The reapers have been cutting grain since dawn, binding it into sheaves, stacking them on the cart. The light is going.
Everyone's tired. The farmer takes one last look across the field, and there, at the far edge, is a sheaf someone missed. A whole bundle of grain, lying in the stubble.
Every instinct says walk back and get it. It's yours. You grew it.

teach.b: In the old Jewish translation: "When thou reapest thy harvest in thy field, and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go back to fetch it; it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow."
The same goes for olives: don't beat the branches a second time. And grapes: don't go back over the vines. What's left belongs to the people who have no field.
The Hebrew name for the forgotten sheaf is shichecha, from the word for forgetting. And here's the odd thing. Many commandments can be planned.
This one can only be kept by accident. Leave a sheaf on purpose and it's a gift, a good one, but it isn't shichecha. Only what you truly forgot counts.

The verse ends with a promise: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thy hands. Rashi, quoting the early midrash, notices how strange that is. Blessed for something you didn't mean to do?
Yes, he says, and how much more for good you do on purpose.
And if a coin falls out of your pocket and a poor person finds it and lives on it, you're blessed through it too.

There's even a story in the Tosefta of a pious man who found he'd forgotten a sheaf, and was so happy to fulfill this commandment that he told his son to bring offerings of thanks. A mistake, turned into a gift.

how: The laws of the forgotten sheaf, the corner of the field and gleanings are set out in the Mishnah's tractate Peah, and some farmers in the land of Israel still observe them; elsewhere they are studied as the root of Jewish giving to the poor.

s: a sheaf left on purpose counts as the forgotten sheaf
only what you truly forgot counts; a planned gift is a different good.
the verse promises a blessing for something done by accident

the forgotten sheaf belongs to the stranger, the orphan and the widow

games.q: it's dusk, the cart is loaded, and you spot a sheaf your workers missed at the far end of your field. what does the Torah say?
o: leave it for the stranger, the orphan and the widow.
games.why: thou shalt not go back to fetch it. a mistake becomes a gift, and a blessing.

practice: Think of something you lost or left behind lately that still stings a little: the umbrella on the train, the twenty that slipped out of your pocket.
Instead of the sting, try the farmer's view: someone may have found it, and needed it. Let it go as a gift you didn't know you were giving.
